nodes.text: Resistivity depends on temperature — usually in metals
(Superconductors — materials with zero resistance — are generally extremely low temperature. “High temperature” superconductors are those which exhibit
above 77 K, the boiling point of nitrogen.)

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: Current equals voltage divided by resistance.
Current equals one over resistance times voltage.

nodes.detailed_figure_description: A coordinate graph has current I on the vertical axis and voltage V on the horizontal axis. Two blue straight lines pass through the origin with positive slopes; one is steep and the other is shallow. The graph illustrates that an ohmic material has a linear current-voltage relationship and that increasing resistance decreases the slope.
nodes.figure_alternative: Current-versus-voltage graph for ohmic materials, showing two straight lines through the origin with different slopes.

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: As resistance increases, the change in current divided by the change in voltage decreases.

nodes.text: In the circuit below, is V higher at point A or B? What about I?

nodes.detailed_figure_description: A single-loop circuit contains a resistor in the top wire and a battery in the bottom wire. Point A is immediately to the left of the resistor, and point B is immediately to its right. An orange arrow above the resistor indicates current I flowing from A toward B. The battery’s positive terminal is on the left and its negative terminal is on the right.
nodes.figure_alternative: Series circuit with current flowing from point A through a resistor to point B; the battery is positive on the left and negative on the right.

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: Voltage equals current times resistance, so the voltage at A is greater than the voltage at B.
